title: Inside Raga: Gaggan Anand's 22-Course Delhi Homecoming With Rydo Anton
excerpt: Anand's first restaurant in India pairs him with his Bangkok head chef of a decade and Zorawar Kalra: one tasting menu, 42 seats at 21A Janpath, and a booking queue that crashed the website on day one.
body:
• Raga, at 21A Janpath Road in New Delhi, is chef Gaggan Anand's first restaurant in India after two decades abroad — a 22-course tasting menu at ₹11,111 per person, before taxes and drinks.
  • The restaurant is a partnership between Anand, his longtime Bangkok head chef Rydo Anton — the "Ra" to Anand's "Ga" in the name — and restaurateur Zorawar Kalra, on the site where Masala Library once stood.
  • Anton, who joined Anand's Bangkok kitchen in 2013 and rose to head chef, leads the kitchen in Delhi; the restaurant serves dinner only, is closed on Tuesdays, and takes its last seating at 9 p.m.
  • Demand has outrun the 42 seats: the restaurant's PR said the booking website drew 7,000 reservation requests on the first day, and tables have sold out weeks ahead.

Twenty years after he left India and built one of the world's most celebrated restaurant careers in Bangkok, Gaggan Anand is cooking at home. Raga, his first restaurant in India, opened on August 26 at 21A Janpath Road, Connaught Place — the address where Zorawar Kalra's Masala Library once stood, next to the Le Méridien hotel. The Hindu's inside account of the restaurant traces how Anand and chef Rydo Anton built it, and what the meal actually involves.

Two Chefs in One Name

The name is a portmanteau with a musical second meaning: "Ra" for Rydo Anton, "Ga" for Gaggan Anand, and a nod to the raga of Indian classical music — a structure with room to improvise, according to The Nod Mag's review. Anton is Indonesian-born; he joined Anand's Bangkok kitchen in 2013, worked his way up to head chef over more than a decade, and is now an equal partner who leads the kitchen at Raga. The third partner is restaurateur Zorawar Kalra of Massive Restaurants. The partners are explicit that Raga is not the Bangkok restaurant transplanted: it works from Indian roots, memories, and emotions, expressed through the pair's own technique.

The Meal

There is one menu: 22 courses at ₹11,111 per person before taxes, with a non-alcoholic pairing at ₹15,111 and a seven-glass wine pairing at ₹18,111, per The Nod Mag's listing. The restaurant seats 42, including a five-seat chef's counter, serves dinner only from 5:30 p.m. with the last seating at 9 p.m., and is closed on Tuesdays, according to EazyDiner's guide. Phones and cameras are put away for most of the meal, and seats are assigned. Reservations are through ragabygaggan.com — and getting one is the hard part: the restaurant's PR said the website crashed under 7,000 reservation requests on the first day, and tables have since sold out more than a month ahead.

Why It Matters

Anand's Bangkok restaurant spent years at the top of Asia's and the world's best-restaurant lists, and his return has been Indian fine dining's longest-running will-he-won't-he story — by his own account, a decade of trying to come back. That he returned not with a copy of the Bangkok original but with a partnership that puts his Indonesian head chef's name alongside his own is the detail reviewers keep circling. Raga is, so far, the rare celebrity-chef homecoming that is also a handover.
